title: Voting Against, Not For
hook: Many voters no longer back a candidate they admire — they vote to keep the other party out. That 'negative partisanship' can make even scandal forgivable.
key_points: Negative partisanship: voters are driven more by dislike of the opposing party than by loyalty to or enthusiasm for their own.
When stopping the other side becomes the goal, a candidate's flaws — even scandals — count for less than the party label.
As polarization deepens, partisans lower the bar for whom they will support, so long as their side wins.
It helps explain how scandal-tainted candidates still win primaries and safe seats.
The dynamic rewards parties for stoking fear of the opponent over making their own positive case.
content_html: It used to be assumed that voters reward the candidate they like best. Increasingly, political scientists argue, the stronger force is the candidate they like least on the other side. This is "negative partisanship": being motivated less by loyalty to your own party than by the desire to keep the rival party from winning.
extra_html: Writing in The Conversation, political scientist Charlie Hunt argues that polarization and negative partisanship have quietly lowered the standards Americans apply to their own side. When the overriding goal is to deny power to the other party, a candidate's personal failings — including scandal — weigh far less than the letter next to their name. That helps explain a pattern that otherwise looks puzzling: candidates dogged by controversy still win primaries and hold safe seats, because their supporters treat the contest as a team loyalty test rather than a referendum on the individual. The dynamic also shapes how parties campaign, rewarding appeals built on fear of the opponent over a positive case for themselves. (U.S. example, though negative partisanship is observed across polarized democracies.)

related.title: Why America Sorts Itself
related.hook: Red places get redder and blue places get bluer. Is it because people move to match their politics — or is politics just one reason among many?

related.title: Populism
related.hook: Populism isn't a single program — it's a style that splits society into two camps: a virtuous 'people' against a corrupt 'elite,' with the populist speaking for the people.

related.title: Public Opinion & Polling
related.hook: What 'the people' think shapes what governments do — but measuring it is trickier than it looks, and a bad poll can mislead as easily as a good one informs.

flashcards.back_html: Being driven more by dislike of the opposing party than by loyalty to or enthusiasm for your own — voting against, not for.

flashcards.prompt: How does negative partisanship help explain support for scandal-prone candidates?

choices.text: When beating the other party is the goal, a candidate's flaws matter less than their party label
Voters stop hearing about scandals once a campaign begins
Scandal-prone candidates spend far more on advertising

flashcards.explanation_html: If the overriding aim is to keep the rival party out, partisans tolerate even a flawed candidate on their own side rather than risk a loss.

flashcards.prompt: What incentive does negative partisanship create for parties?

choices.text: To stoke fear of the opponent rather than make their own positive case
To move toward the political center to win swing voters

flashcards.explanation_html: When votes hinge on fear of the other side, attacking the rival can be more effective than offering one's own appeal.
